doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

chapter: Making a living: studio and odd work
title: A blue-collar musician who never turns down work
summary: He never refused work, which he thinks dissipates creativity, and learned from bad gigs, citing Art Tatum.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: I was going to say, what was the job where you said man I can’t believe I’m doing this. Has there been one?

Well I’ve never, from as early on as I can remember, before I was even in the union, just a kid playing in high school gyms and stuff, I never turned down work. I think I must have figured out very early on that you better not turn down work, because there may not be any next week. And still to this day I find it very difficult to turn something down, unless it’s just absolutely not right. I mean I’ve always been kind of a blue collar musician. I mean I work and I think really it’s a detriment in some ways, because you dissipate your energies and your creativity to a certain extent by taking that approach to the business. I think a truer artistic approach, where you only do, as guys I’ve known, who only do what they want to do, only do what they feel is pure and untainted and artistically correct, if you can survive doing that I think it is better in a lot of ways. Because I think you save your energies for that focus. If you’re doing too many different kinds of things in this business I think it’s very hard to stay focused. And so there is a down side to that work ethic.
Well I know what you’re talking about.
You know what I mean exactly.

And you can get a lot of calls to do lots of different kinds of things, and perhaps the thing that you are looking to really excel at does suffer a bit, but as you said there’s a practical side to life that requires you to take those things, because they’re paying.

Well if you’re raising a family and here again if you’re single and are in a different situation you have a lot more freedom to say no. But for various reasons I just have always felt, hey if the phone rings, it might be foolish to turn it down. So I’ve done a lot of things. So anyway in answer to your question, I’d never felt like I was above doing a certain kind of job. The only thing that’s ever bummed me, like with all of us I guess, is when it turns out that it’s really bad, just the playing is bad, if it’s a horrible singer you end up with for four hours accompanying or just a band that’s hopeless or whatever, then you’re just waiting for it to be over and you’re thinking maybe why did I get into this. But we all go through those experiences. And a lot of times coming up I was lucky to be even in that good a band because I was still learning myself and as Art Tatum, I remember he said in an interview I heard a few years ago on the radio, that he had never heard a pianist he couldn’t learn from, which is kind of the same thing. I mean you’re going to learn from even the worst situations.
Yeah. You can learn what not to do also.
What not to do or avoid, or how not to play.
